paragraphs.text: [?] (Latin version by Zinus [?]). The president of this Church, and the teachers of unerring piety and of the virtuous way of life, are very like schoolmasters, who teach children their first letters. They take from their fathers children who are still infants and lisping, and they do not lead them straight to the more advanced lessons. First they trace alpha on the wax tablet, and then the letters that follow, and teach the children to know their names and train their hands on the written shapes. After this they move them on to syllables, and next they teach them how to pronounce words. In the same way the leaders of the Church first bring the hearer to the elementary lessons, and only then give him knowledge of the more advanced. Over the past two days we have disciplined the pleasure-seeking of the throat and the belly. So do not think that today too I shall say the usual things: that it is good to despise meat, to abstain from wine that stirs up laughter and revelry, to hold back the cooks, and to let the wine-pourer's hand rest from its labour. I have said these things often enough, and you have shown by your actions that the advice took effect. Now that you have been trained in the first lesson, it is good to lead you on step by step and give you the greater and more manly teachings that remain. There is also a bodiless fasting, an immaterial self-control: an abstinence from evils that concerns the soul. It is for the sake of this fasting that this abstinence from foods was also laid down for us. So fast from wickedness; ex-

ercise self-control over the desire for what belongs to others; abstain from unjust gain; starve to death the avarice of Mammon; let there be nothing stored in your house that was gained by violence and robbery. What use is it if you do not put meat into your mouth, but bite your brother with wickedness? What do you gain if you do not eat your own food, but unjustly take what belongs to the poor man? What kind of piety is it if you drink water but plot [?] deceit, and thirst for blood out of malice? Judas surely fasted with the eleven too. But he did not tame his love of money, and so his going without food did him no good for salvation. The devil does not eat either, for he is a bodiless spirit; yet he fell from the heights through wickedness. In the same way none of the demons takes delicacies, and none can be charged with heavy drinking or drunkenness, because their nature has cut them off from taking food. Yet night and day they wander through the air as makers and servants of wickedness, and they work zealously at their plots against us. They waste away with envy and malice. We would do well to flee these vices if we human beings are to be akin to God, since the demons lost their kinship with the good. So let a philosophic way of life guide the lives of Christians, and let the soul flee the harm that wickedness does. If we abstain from wine and meat but are guilty of deliberate sins, I tell you beforehand and solemnly declare that water, vegetables and a bloodless table will do us no good, because our inner disposition does not match our outward appearance. Fasting was laid down for the purity of the soul. But if the soul is defiled by its choices and its other actions, why do we waste the water we drink for nothing? Why [?] cultivate so much mud that cannot be washed away? What is the use of bodily fasting if the mind is not pure? It is no use for the chariot [?] to be sturdy and the four-horse team well trained if the driver is mad. And what is the use of a well-built ship if the helmsman is drunk? Fasting is the foundation of virtue. But the foundation of a house and the keel of a ship are useless and worthless, however firmly they are laid, unless the rest is skilfully built on top of them. In the same way this self-control is no use unless the rest of righteousness is joined to it and follows from it. Let the fear of God teach the tongue to say what is fitting and not to speak idle words; to know the right times and measures, and necessary speech, and an apt reply; not to speak without measure, and not to hail down vehement words on those it meets. This is why the very thin membrane that ties the tongue to the lower jaw is called the bridle: so that the tongue may not utter disorderly and unregulated things. Let it bless and not revile; let it sing psalms and not blaspheme; let it speak well of others and not slander them. And let the reckless hand be bound by the remembrance of God as if by a chain. This is why we fast: because insults and blows abused our Lamb before

the nails. So let us, the disciples of Christ, not imitate the Jewish way. If that is how we behave, Isaiah will say to us: "Why do you fast for lawsuits and quarrels, and strike the lowly with your fists?" Learn from the same prophet what a guileless and pure fast does: "Loose every bond of injustice; untie the knots of forced contracts. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house." The present time has brought us a great many naked and homeless people. A crowd of captives stands at everyone's door. There is no lack of strangers and exiles either, and everywhere you can see a hand stretched out, begging. The open air is their house. Their lodgings are porticoes, alleys and the more deserted corners of the marketplace. Like night-ravens and owls they lurk in holes. Their clothing is patched and tattered rags. Their farming is the goodwill of those who pity them. Their food is whatever happens to fall their way from someone they meet. Their drink comes from springs, as for the beasts. Their cup is the hollow of their hands. Their storehouse is the fold of their garment, provided it is not torn and holds what is put into it. Their table is their knees pressed together; their bed is the ground; their bath is a river or a lake, which God gave to all in common and without craftsmanship. Their life is wandering and wild. It was not like this from the beginning; misfortune and necessity made it so. Help these people, you who fast. Be generous towards your unfortunate brothers. Give to the hungry what you have taken away from your own belly. Let the fear of God be a just equalizer [?]. With prudent self-control, heal two opposite ailments: your own surfeit and your brother's hunger. Physicians do the same: they empty some patients and fill others, so that each one's health is managed by adding and taking away. Be persuaded by good advice. Let my word open the doors of the wealthy. Let this counsel bring the poor man in to the man who has. Yet let it not be a single word of mine that enriches those who groan. Let the eternal Word of God give them a house, a bed and a table. With a word to your servants, provide from your possessions what they need. Besides these, there are other poor people who are sick and bedridden. Let each of you look carefully after his neighbours. Do not let the person near you be cared for by someone else. Do not let another take the treasure that lies right beside you. Embrace the afflicted person like gold. Take the sufferer in your arms as you would your own health, or the safety of your wife, your children, your servants and your whole household. PATROL. GR. XLVI.

The poor man who is sick is doubly poor. The destitute who are healthy go from door to door and walk up to those who have. They sit at the crossroads and call out to everyone passing by. But those who are fettered by disease are shut up in cramped lodgings and narrow corners, like Daniel in the pit, and they wait for you, the devout lover of the poor, as Daniel waited for Habakkuk. Become the Prophet's companion through almsgiving: be quick to bring food, and stand by the needy without hesitating. Giving is no loss. Do not be afraid: the fruit of almsgiving springs up in abundance. Sow by giving, and you will fill your house with good sheaves. But you will say, "I am poor too." So be it; granted. Give what you have, for God does not ask for what is beyond your power. You give a loaf [?], another a cup of wine, another a garment, and so the misfortune of one person is relieved by everyone's contribution. Moses did not receive the cost of the tabernacle from a single donor either, but from the whole people. The rich man brought him gold, another man silver, the poor man skins, and the one poorer than the poor brought hair. Do you see how the widow's penny surpassed the offerings of the rich? She emptied out all she had, while from them only a little fell away. Do not despise those who lie on the ground as if they were worth nothing. Consider who they are, and you will find their dignity: they have put on the person of our Saviour. For the Lover of mankind lent them his own person, so that through it they might shame the hard-hearted and those who hate the poor. They are like people who hold up the emperor's images against those who use violence against them, so that by the ruler's likeness they may shame the man who despises them. These are the stewards of the good things we hope for. They are the doorkeepers of the kingdom, who open the doors to the kind and shut them on the harsh and the misanthropic. They are both fierce accusers and good advocates. They defend and accuse not by speaking but by being seen by the Judge. What is done to them cries out before the One who knows hearts more clearly than any herald. It is on their account that the fearful judgement seat of God, which you have often heard about, was written down for us through the angels [?]. For I saw there the Son of Man coming from heaven, treading the air as if it were ground, and escorted by many myriads of angels. Then I saw a throne of glory raised up, and the whole human race, all who have ever come into being, been lit by the sun and breathed this air, separated into two

groups and standing before the judgement seat. Those on the right were called lambs, and I heard those on the other side called goats; each had drawn the name upon themselves through the likeness of their ways. There were exchanges between the Judge and those being judged, and replies from those called to account to the King. Each was allotted what was fitting: those who had lived the best life received the enjoyment of the kingdom; the misanthropic and the wicked received punishment by fire, and everlasting punishment at that. The word records all this carefully, and the judgement seat was painted for us precisely by the word for no other reason than that we might learn the goodness of beneficence. For beneficence is what holds life together. It is the mother of the poor, the teacher of the rich, a good nurse of children and carer of the old, the storehouse of the needy, the common harbour of the unfortunate, and it shares out its care to every age and every misfortune. Those who preside over vain contests announce their generosity with a trumpet and proclaim a distribution of wealth to everyone in the wrestling-school. In the same way beneficence calls to itself all who are in difficulties and distress, and it gives those who come to it not rewards for blows but cures for misfortunes. It is higher than any praiseworthy deed. It sits beside God, it is a friend of the good, and it has a close kinship with him. That is why God himself is shown to us as the first to perform good and kind deeds. The creation of the earth, the ordering of the heavens, the orderly succession of the seasons, the heat of the sun, the chilling formation of ice and everything else in particular, God does not do for himself [?], since he has no need of such things. He works continually for us: the invisible farmer of human food, the timely sower and the skilled irrigator. For, as Isaiah says, he gives seed to the sower. He sprinkles water from the clouds gently on the earth at one time, and at another pours it violently down the furrows. When the crops have grown and the green stage is past, he scatters the clouds from the whole sky and then sets the sun over the crops with nothing to cover it, stretching out its hot, fiery rays so that the ears of grain may ripen for the harvest. He also tends the vine, preparing drink in its season for the thirsty. He raises herds of various kinds for us, so that people may have meat in abundance; the hides of some grow wool to give us covering, and those of others are made into our shoes. You see that God is the first lover of beneficence: as was said before, he feeds the hungry, gives drink to the thirsty and clothes the naked.

If you want to hear how he also heals the afflicted, learn this. Who taught the bee to make wax, and honey along with it? Who made the pine, the terebinth and the mastic tree drip that rich sap? Who made the land of the Indians the mother of dry and fragrant fruits? Who made the olive grow as a help against bodily toil and pain? Who gave us the ability to tell roots and herbs apart, and knowledge of their properties? Who established medicine, the art that produces health? Who sent up springs of hot water from the earth, some to heal what is cold and moist in us, others to loosen what is dry or hardened? It is fitting at this point to quote Baruch as well: "He found out every way of knowledge, and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved." This is why there are arts that work with fire, others without fire, and others in water, and countless inventions of crafts, so that the needs of life may be served without lack. This is what God is like, the first inventor of beneficence, the rich and compassionate provider of what we need. But we, who are taught by every letter of Scripture to imitate our own Lord and Creator as far as a mortal can imitate the blessed and immortal One, sweep everything off for our own enjoyment. Some things we allot to our own lives, and others we store up for our heirs. Of the unfortunate we take no account, and we give no kindly thought to the poor. What a pitiless attitude! A man sees another man lacking bread, without the food that is needed to keep the spark of life alive. Yet he does not help him gladly or reach out to save him. He looks past him as if he were a flourishing plant pitifully withering for lack of water, and all the while he has an overflowing abundance and could channel comfort from his possessions to many. The flow of a single spring enriches many broad plains, and in the same way the wealth of a single house is enough to save whole crowds of the poor, provided that a stingy and unsharing attitude does not fall like a stone into the channel and block the flow. Let us not live wholly for the flesh; let us live a little for God too. The sensation and enjoyment of food serves only a small part of the flesh, the throat. Once it has made the food rot in the belly, it ends up in the privy. But mercy and beneficence are things dear to God, and in whatever person they dwell, they make him godlike and shape him into an imitation of the good, so that

he becomes an image of the first, pure Being that surpasses every mind. And what result do they promise for our efforts? In this life, a good hope and a joyful expectation. Hereafter, when we have put off this perishing flesh and put on incorruption, a blessed life, unending and indestructible, prepared in wonderful delights that are not yet known to us. So you who were created rational, and who have the mind as interpreter and teacher of divine things, do not be lured by what is temporary. Acquire the things that never abandon the one who has acquired them. Set limits to the way you use the means of life. Not everything is yours; let a part belong also to the poor, who are beloved of God. For all things belong to God, the common Father, and we are brothers, being of one race. For brothers, the best and most just thing is to share the inheritance in equal portions. Second best, even if one or two of them take the larger share, the rest should at least receive a part. But if someone wants to be lord of absolutely everything, and keeps his brothers from even a third or a fifth share, he is a bitter tyrant, an implacable barbarian, an insatiable beast that gapes with pleasure over the feast by itself. Or rather, he is fiercer than the beasts themselves. For a wolf lets another wolf share its prey, and many dogs tear at one carcass together; but the insatiable man lets none of his own kind share in his wealth. A moderate table is enough for you. Do not drift out onto the open sea of unbridled feasting. The shipwreck that threatens there is a grievous one. It does not break you on hidden rocks; it casts you out into the deepest darkness, from which no one who has fallen in ever [?]

Use, but do not misuse; Paul taught you this too. Allow yourself measured enjoyment. Do not revel madly in pleasures. Do not simply become the destroyer of every living thing: four-footed creatures large and small, birds and fish, the easily caught and the rare, the cheap and the costly. Do not fill one belly with the sweat of many hunters, like a very deep well that many hands throwing in earth cannot fill. Because of those who live in luxury, not even the depths of the sea are left in peace. It is not only the fish swimming in the water that are caught. Even the wretched creatures that live in the sediment at the bottom are dragged up onto land and into this air. So the various kinds of oysters have not escaped notice: the sea urchin is hunted, the creeping cuttlefish is netted, the octopus clinging to the rocks is torn away, and shellfish are dragged up from the lowest depths. And all kinds of

creatures, those that swim in the waves at the surface and those whose lot is to live on the sea floor, are brought up into this air, while the ingenuity of the pleasure-lovers devises all sorts of [?] against them.

And what comes next among those who live in luxury? Wherever the disease of vice strikes, it inevitably draws after it the materials that go with it. That is why those who lay a pampered, Sybaritic table are inevitably drawn into building grandiose houses, and spend their great wealth on the size of their homes and on elaborate decoration. On top of this they adorn their couches and pile them with flowered and richly embroidered fabrics. They have tables forged from many talents of silver, some beaten smooth, others decorated with carving, so that the eye can feast on the scenes along with the throat. Consider with me what follows: mixing bowls, tripods, jars, pouring vessels, serving dishes, countless kinds of drinking cups; jesters, mimes, lyre-players, singers, clever talkers, musicians male and female, dancing girls, the whole string of debauchery; boys made effeminate by their long hair, shameless girls, sisters of Herodias in indecency, who kill John, that is, the godlike and philosophic mind in each person. While all this is going on in the house, countless Lazaruses sit at the gate. Some are grievously covered in sores, others have had an eye gouged out, others groan over their mutilated feet, and some of them can only crawl, having lost the use of all their limbs. They cry out but are not heard, for the sound of the pipes drowns them out, along with the tunes of the songs [?] and the cackling of loud laughter. And if they bother the doors any further, the merciless master's insolent porter leaps out from somewhere and drives them off with sticks, calling them shameless dogs and scraping their wounds with whips. So the friends of Christ, who are the chief concern of the commandments, go away. They have received not a scrap of bread or any food to go with it, and have gained insults and blows into the bargain. Meanwhile, inside the workshop of Mammon, some are belching up food like overloaded ships spilling bilge, and others have fallen asleep on the table with the cups standing beside them. A double sin lives in that unseemly house: one in the surfeit of the drunkards, the other in the hunger of the poor who were driven away. If God sees these things, as he certainly does, what end to your life do you expect, you haters of the poor? Tell me, do you not know that it is because of such people that the holy Gospel cries out and testifies with all its terrifying and fearful examples? It is written that the man raised in fine linen roars and groans heavily, held fast in the abyss of evils; another

[?] And again the man of like character to him was condemned to an unexpected death: in the evening he was planning his morning meal, and he did not live to see the first ray of dawn. Let us not be mortal in faith and immortal in our enjoyment. For this is how we think, we who want to grant everything to the flattery of the flesh: as though we were masters of houses who would have no successors, as though we were lords of earthly things forever. In summer we worry about the sowing, and at the sowing we hope for the delight of the harvest. We plant the plane tree and hope for the shade of the tall tree; we set the date stone in the ground and wait for the sweetness of its fruit. And we often do this in gray old age, when the winter of death is near, and what is left of life is not a cycle of years but three or four days. Let us reason, then, as reasoning beings, that our life is passing and our time flows away, unstable and unchecked, like the current of a river, driving everything in it toward the end of its course. And would that, being brief and perishable, it were also free from accountability! But this is where the danger lies: that for every hour, and indeed for the words we speak, we owe a defense before the incorruptible tribunal. That is why the blessed Psalmist too, turning his mind to thoughts like those we are now expressing, longs to know the appointed time of his own end. He earnestly begs God to be taught the number of his remaining days, so that he may prepare himself for the works needed for his departure, and not be suddenly thrown into confusion, like an unprepared traveler who is halfway along the road and still searching for the provisions he needs. So he says: "Make known to me, Lord, my end, and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what I lack. Behold, you have made my days a few handbreadths, and my existence is as nothing before you." See the good concern of a wise soul, and that while holding royal rank! For he sees in a mirror the King of kings and the Judge of judges, and he seeks to gain the perfect adornment of the commandments and so depart complete, a citizen of the life there. May we all attain that life by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
